title: A request has a method, a path and headers

terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. run.js starts the cupboard server, runs your functions against it and prints every request and answer.

tasks.title: Write the first line of a request
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1` in `src/requests.js`, make `requestLine(method, address)` give back the first line of the request that asks for `address` with `method`, as text: the method in capital letters, a space, the path with its question mark part, a space, and `HTTP/1.1`. For example `'GET /shows?day=saturday HTTP/1.1'`.

Check calls `requestLine` with methods and addresses of its own, some in small letters, some with a question mark part and one with no path at all.
nextSteps: Run `node run.js` and look at the first line under any request: that is the shape to build.
Make a `URL` from the address and find the property that holds the question mark part.
Put the method in capitals, the path and its question mark part, and the version together.
Run `node run.js` again and compare both Task 1 lines with the addresses they came from.
hints: The host is not on the first line of a request. It travels in a header of its own, so the line only needs what comes after the host.
A `URL` has `pathname` for the path and `search` for the question mark part, `?` included, or `''` when there is none. Text has a method that turns it into capitals.
Build it with a template literal: `${method.toUpperCase()} ${url.pathname}${url.search} HTTP/1.1`.

tasks.title: Remove a song request
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, make `removeRequest(base, id)` ask the server at `base` to remove song request number `id`. The request goes to the path `/requests/<id>`, with the method that removes. It gives back the text of the answer's body, whatever the server says.

Check starts a server of its own and looks at both sides: the method and path of the request its server received, and the text `removeRequest` gave back.
nextSteps: Build the address of the song request from `base` and `id`.
Find in the lesson the method that removes, and how to hand a method to `fetch`.
Wait for the answer and give back its body text.
Run `node run.js`: the cupboard server answers, but it does not remove the request yet.
hints: Given only an address, `fetch` sends a GET, which asks to read. To do anything else, it needs to be told the method.
`fetch` takes a second value: an object of options. One of them is `method`.
`await fetch(address, { method: 'DELETE' })`, where `address` is built from `base` and `` `/requests/${id}` ``.

tasks.title: Say who is asking
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, make `removeAsStudio(base, id, key)` send the same request as `removeRequest`, with one header more: `authorization`, whose value is the word `Bearer`, a space and `key`. It gives back the text of the answer's body.

Check starts a server of its own, calls `removeAsStudio` with a key of its own, and looks at the method, path and `authorization` header its server received, and at the text that came back.
nextSteps: Start from what you wrote for Task 2.
Add `headers` to the options you hand `fetch`.
Build the value of the header from the word, a space and `key`.
Run `node run.js`: with the studio key the request comes off the list, with a wrong key it stays.
hints: A header is a name and a value. The server finds it by its name, spelt exactly, so `authorisation` with an s is a different header that it never looks at.
The options of `fetch` can have `headers`: an object whose property names are header names and whose values are text.
Hand `fetch` the options `{ method: 'DELETE', headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${key}` } }`, with the value written as a template literal.

tasks.title: Ask for a kind of answer
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 4`, make `fetchAs(base, path, type)` ask the server at `base` for the page at `path` with a GET request whose `accept` header is `type`, like `'text/html'`. It gives back the text of the answer's body.

Check starts a server of its own, calls `fetchAs` with paths and types of its own, and looks at the `accept` header its server received and at the text that came back.
nextSteps: Hand `fetch` a header called `accept` with `type` as its value.
Wait for the answer and give back its body text.
Run `node run.js`: the same page comes back as HTML for one call and as plain text for the other.
hints: Without your header, `fetch` still sends `accept: */*`, which means any kind will do. Your header takes its place.
This is the same shape as Task 3: `headers` in the options of `fetch`, with a different name and value. A GET needs no method in the options.
`await fetch(new URL(path, base), { headers: { accept: type } })`, then give back the body text.
